newsitem.title: GERMANY: German sick pay dispute highly symbolic for unions.
newsitem.headline: German sick pay dispute highly symbolic for unions.

text.p: Germany's bitter sick pay dispute, which sparked off a wave of wildcat strikes at car factories on Tuesday, means far more to the country's trade unions than just the paid leave or few extra marks at issue.

The 20 percent cut in benefits, which has just gone into effect as part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity package, represents to union leaders an historic reversal of gains they made during the "economic miracle" of the booming 1950s.

They see the full pay that workers used to get when they called in sick as the first line of defence against the looming rollback of the comfortable welfare state built up in prosperous West Germany after World War Two.
"Almost no other issue can motivate workers more to strike," said Klaus Kehrmann, a benefits specialist with the German Trade Union Federation (DGB).

Under the new law, workers will get only 80 percent of their full pay for the first six weeks of illness. If they want, they can give up one of their 30 annual vacation days to compensate for each week of absence.
Employers, backed by Kohl, argued the old full pay system invited misuse, especially by workers who just wanted a free day now and then.
The unions angrily denied the charge and also cried "hands off" their hard-won holidays, which like the sick benefits are among the most generous in the world.

But statistics showing sick leave was considerably higher in Germany than in countries with less generous systems did not exactly help the unions' case. Companies with more strict sick leave benefits also showed fewer workers calling in sick.

West German workers won the right to six weeks of full pay for sick leave during a gruelling 16-week strike in 1956-1957, the longest ever held in a country where consensus between labour and capital has been the norm.
Metal workers in Schleswig-Holstein, the poorest state in West Germany, struck through the winter to win the concession, which became the benchmark for wage agreements elsewhere.
This was a milestone for blue-collar workers since it finally brought them up to the same level as white-collar employees, who won full sick pay as far back as 1861.
It came during the postwar "economic miracle," when annual growth rates were over seven percent and the working week began falling from a high of almost 50 hours in the early 1950s.
That strike by IG Metall, the world's largest union, has become almost legendary in postwar labour relations for the solidarity workers showed and new tactics their leaders used.
Instead of a blanket strike, the union opted for "flexible escalation," staging selective walkouts to add pressure on managers who saw competitors continuing to produce as normal.
This is now the standard tactic that German unions use at the start of a pay dispute.
During the long strike, IG Metall hired cinemas to show idle workers films and where popular cabaret artists performed.
It even organised coffee mornings for workers' wives so they could get away from disgruntled husbands moping around home with nothing to do.

Trade union leaders say that showdown also secured the social consensus that has given German workers a high standard of living and helped German industry to record one of the lowest strike records in the world.
"Full sick pay benefits are a pillar of our welfare state," Herbert Mai, head of the OeTV public service workers union, said recently.
